report.executive_summary: All four robot cell packages pass both client gates, so WO-04 reduces to measured energy on the shared acceptance-batch basis. The verified ladder is P1 6 kWh, P3 14, P2 40, P4 67, giving gaps of +8, +34 and +61 kWh over the minimum. The energy-first policy selects P1, 8 kWh (2.33x) below runner-up P3. Quality is informational once the 80 gate is cleared: P4's perfect 100 arrives with the worst energy at 11.17x the minimum. Defect margins invert that picture: P1 and P3 carry 1/5 defects with four defects of headroom, while P2 and P4 sit at the 5/5 ceiling where any added defect disqualifies. Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability remain unverified and are excluded from ranking.
report.figure_caption: WO-04 handover view: energy ladder for all four qualifying packages on the shared batch basis, with the P1-minimum reference line, gap callouts, cost ratios and defect-headroom chips.

recommendation.rationale: P1. All four clear both gates; P1's 6 kWh is lowest, 8 kWh (2.33x) below runner-up P3 on the identical batch basis. Its 1/5 defects leave four of headroom, so it is the most robust qualifier too. P4's 100 quality is informational above the 80 gate and cannot offset 11.17x energy. Fallback: P3 at 14 kWh; P2 and P4 sit at the 5/5 ceiling.

sections.body: The policy qualifies any package with quality at least 80 and a raw defect count at most 5, then minimizes energy, using candidate ID only to break ties. Against the trusted table: quality reads P4 100, P1 98, P3 89, P2 86, all above 80; defects read P1 1, P3 1, P2 5, P4 5, all within the ceiling. All four qualify, so nothing is rejected, and the tie-break never engages because the energy readings are distinct. The decision therefore rests entirely on the energy column; the eligibility test only sets the field.
sections.heading: Gates and eligibility

sections.body: Measured energy orders the field P1 6 < P3 14 < P2 40 < P4 67 kWh. The winning margin over P3 is 8 kWh; P3 to P2 adds 26; P2 to P4 adds 27. Relative to P1, P3 costs 2.33x, P2 6.67x and P4 11.17x the minimum. Spacing drives sensitivity: P3 is close enough that a large measurement error or a defect finding could change the outcome, whereas P2 and P4 trail by 34 and 61 kWh and are unreachable under any admissible re-measurement. All readings share one acceptance batch, output and load, so no cross-basis correction applies.
sections.heading: Energy ladder, gaps and cost ratios

sections.body: Defect positions invert the intuitive quality story. P1 (quality 98, 1/5) and P3 (89, 1/5) each keep four defects of headroom; P2 (86, 5/5) and P4 (100, 5/5) sit exactly at the ceiling, so a single added defect disqualifies them. The winner is therefore the most robust candidate on both axes at once. The natural fallback is P3 at 14 kWh, equally robust on defects; it takes the win only if P1 is disqualified by new defect findings or an invalidated measurement. P2 and P4 are fragile fallbacks: with zero headroom, any defect regression disqualifies them, and they cost 6.67x and 11.17x the minimum besides.
sections.heading: Defect margins and fallback robustness

sections.body: Four items remain questions, not findings. First, measurement uncertainty on the 6 kWh reading is not supplied; the 8 kWh margin to P3 absorbs it only if the combined error stays below half that gap. Second, cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability are unverified; only the client can admit them, and nothing supplied justifies overriding measured energy. Third, whether the shared acceptance-batch basis persists into future work orders is unconfirmed; a changed basis requires re-measurement, not extrapolation. Fourth, defect stability for P2 and P4 matters only if either becomes a fallback; at the 5/5 ceiling both are fragile, which does not affect P1 today.
sections.heading: Open questions and unverified factors
